Movistar Game Club · Intern Service Designer · 2024

Movistar Game Club

Scenario

Movistar Game Club is part of a pioneering esports and video game entertainment producer in Colombia. They make experiences for every kind of gamer, from casual players to professionals and the people who watch, by running gaming center activations, building teams, and connecting content creators with academies, tournaments, and regular rental hours.

Problem

People don’t attend the center because of the high prices, and prefer to stay home. The venue sells hours of equipment, but the community doesn’t resonate with that business model.

Why was I hired?

To analyze the first 3 months of operations and to research (interviews, surveys, maps), assisting and prototyping with the goal of bringing in more people.

My contribution

I researched and revealed how people visit the venue for the community, the atmosphere and the feeling of belonging. I designed events around what happens beyond the competition: where spectators connect, communities come together, and shared experiences create belonging. I also worked on the backstage, to see how efficiently we can create an event.

Research · regular events

Competitions focused on prizes for the winner.

Key finding: the community wasn’t looking for a competitive landscape. Regular tournaments are dominated by the same players, who live off them. The different levels make the tournaments frustrating, and regular players stop going after 2 events.

For the initial events, the purpose was to standardize event organization with clear tasks along the way. I was expected to highlight friction points during organization and realization.

Persona · “Esports team fan”

Juan, 16

LoL fan · Aspiring competitor · Introverted · Forum participant

Juan lives in northern Bogotá with his parents. In his free time he watches Twitch and plays LoL with friends online, whom he met through streamer fandoms and forums on Discord or Reddit. He especially loves competition and never misses one for the team.

Key needs

Tension grows at home during events because of noise and crowds late at night. A place with in-person watch parties would make Juan a very likely user.

Interview takeaways

People refused to go to the venue by themselves for competitions.

“the gang gets together”

The moment when the community meets people they already know creates a sense of belonging — the highest-leverage moment found in our interview process.

Players come for a pro experience, not just competition. Pro-level conditions, expert casting and a cheering crowd turn a tournament into a moment amateur players remember — and that feeling makes them want to improve and come back.

How might we make every amateur player feel like they’re on a pro stage, from the setup to the casting to the crowd?

Synthesis of research

A stakeholder map, used to see every task and its actor. It allowed us to see the full flow between different teams, especially teams that don’t know each other.

Current system

The community manager (CM) was connected to almost everyone, so messages to brands, influencers and activations competed with logistics. The CM couldn’t multitask, which made the rest of the team rush.

Proposed system

I redesigned the CM flow: rebalanced the CM’s tasks, distributed the rest, focused the CM on brands, and integrated communication so every member is aware of each task.

Events focus on viewers · changing the focus of the competition

Proposed system

Developed two events focused on the viewer, not the player: Fortnite × Metallica and the Leviathan watch party (exclusivity). We built a full area of activities and displays, and tested a new task plan for creating these events.

500+attendees and 1M+ impressions

130+hours rented during events

Savannah Philharmonic Orchestra · SCAD · Spring 2025

A concert night that pays for itself

Give the loyal audience back the high-deluxe experience they share with the orchestra, without losing the venue’s purpose, which in the end is to make a profit, and honor those who love the music, not only the tourists.

My roleResearch lead

I led the team’s research: Sav Phil’s annual reports and ProPublica financials, a 17-student survey, the interview with the Executive Director, and the stakeholder and ecosystem mapping.

My roleCo-creation workshop lead

I led the blueprinting workshop with front- and back-stage actors: three stations, a simulated concert night and MoSCoW sorting. It confirmed four issues.

With Lucas Qin, Maisie Moore and Rhian Sterling · four students · April–May 2025

01

The key issue

Context

Sav Phil is a mid-sized regional orchestra with a yearly budget of about $2M. It plays the Lucas Theatre — 1,267 seats — at $25 to $90 a ticket, and was still recovering from COVID. It wants “Music for All”, but modernizing risks alienating the loyal audience that has always filled its seats.

The gap

70% of revenue comes from donations and 30% from tickets. Each concert costs about $100K and the most tickets can bring in is about $50K, so every concert runs a gap of around $50K that donations have to cover.

$50K

gap on every concert: about $100K of cost against about $50K of maximum ticket revenue

70/30

donations against tickets, as a share of revenue

80%+

of the audience we observed was 60 or older

Figures from Sav Phil’s annual reports and ProPublica financials; the audience share is our own observation at concerts.

The economics of one concert

Cost
$100K
Tickets, max
$50K
Gap
$50K

Per concert, approximate. A full Lucas Theatre at $25–90 a ticket cannot cover what a concert costs; donations close the gap every time.

How might we maintain Sav Phil’s values and long-term goals while addressing pressing concerns?

02

The ecosystem

Three key stages carry the loyalty story: how guests discover the Phil, how they arrive, and why they come back.

A six-stage patron journey, from first hearing about a concert to coming back for the next one. An ecosystem map tied every stakeholder to the touchpoints they own. These are the three stages I followed most closely.

  1. 1AwarenessPublicity · email from marketing · word of mouth
  2. 2RegisterTicketing through the SCAD box office · no delivery option
  3. 3ArrivalParking · main gate · ticket scan and security · 10’
  4. 4EngageLobby: program note, bar, souvenirs · the performance · 90’
  5. 5ExitUshers out · pick up bag and souvenir · 10’
  6. 6Loyalty“Thank you for coming” · post-concert feedback · stamps
Stage 1Awareness

Customers learn about the Savannah Philharmonic from various sources. The orchestra’s core team help raise awareness through outreach and promotional events.

Stage 3Arrival

Customers arrive at the venue. They receive their tickets, wait in line, and take their seats. The orchestra staff greets the audience.

Stage 6Loyalty

Donation programs and social events build deeper connections with the customers. Marketing and executive teams can foster ongoing engagement and loyalty.

03

Ellie’s night

To feel the experience from the inside, we followed Ellie, a concertgoer, from ticket to applause. Her emotional curve shows where the night works and where it hurts most: a double-booked seat.

Persona

Ellie Thornton, 73

Season patronThe audience Sav Phil already has

The most painful moment

06 · Seat conflict — Ellie is distressed. The volunteer walks her to her seat and season ticket holders are already sitting there. The seat is double booked.

04

The co-creation workshop

I led it. We tested our research with front- and back-stage actors in a blueprinting workshop. It confirmed four issues:

1Double booking: one seat, two ticket holders
2Human error: friends meant to sit together
3Ticket pickup: digital vs physical ticket confusion
4Music engagement: guessing a piece’s background

The workshop put the three pillars — financial stability, community engagement and artistic excellence — in front of the stakeholders and asked them to work through three stations:

Education & outreach

Talk about what Sav Phil does in the community, and ask the stakeholders about their pain points and perspectives.

Financial stability

Play a money game: the stakeholders decide where they think the money would be best used.

Artistic excellence

Play music for the stakeholders to get them engaged, and ask what they think of the pieces being played.

A simulated concert

I led the workshop. Stakeholders walked through a simulated concert night to find the pain points where they happen, ideated on the spot, and sorted the ideas with MoSCoW: must, should, could, won’t.

Five opportunity areas

Themed concerts
Interactive experiences
Souvenirs & a stamp collection for loyalty
Educational music classes
Stronger digital promotion
05

The future-state blueprint

A deluxe night for loyal audiences that still pays its way, from guided parking to the final applause. Orange marks what changes.

Future-state touches

Parking serviceOptional ticket pickupGuided seatingClear ticket infoProgram notesStamp-collection souvenirsBaggage depositLobby barSubtitlesLocker pick-upPost-concert feedback

A deluxe night for the audience that has always filled the seats, that still pays its way.

More of the research behind the story+

Industry context

The orchestral and performing-arts sector is in a transformative period: shifting demographics, digital disruption and a re-evaluation of cultural equity. Ticket revenue has passed pre-pandemic levels, but patrons attend less often, and the traditional subscriber base is aging.

2025 was an important year for Sav Phil: the last year to fulfill its strategic plan. Operational inefficiencies, accessibility barriers and limited publicity had reduced its ability to deliver on its goal of “Music for All”, on and off the stage.

Top challenges reported by U.S. orchestras. Source: League of American Orchestras, as compiled in our white paper.

What we discovered

The pressing problems weren’t on stage. They were around the ticket.

I led the research. We mapped the stakeholders — board, staff, donors, volunteers, musicians, locals, media and local businesses — and how board, staff and volunteers actually interact with each other. The 17 SCAD students we surveyed barely knew Sav Phil and had little interest in classical music.

The interview with the Executive Director verified four operational problems that patrons feel directly. None of them is about the music.

The four verified problems:

TicketingRuns through the SCAD box office, not the orchestra’s own channel.
SeatingDouble seating, caused by user error.
Season holdersSay they won’t come, then show up.
DeliveryNo ticket delivery option.

From the primary and secondary research, four findings about the audience itself:

Alienated traditionalists

Modernization pushes away traditional art lovers.

Disconnected youth

Young audiences feel boredom through traditional practices.

Lack of modernization

“There’s a gentle resistance to change, where tradition still guides the structure, but the rhythm of the present has yet to be fully embraced.”

Confusing music

Lack of context in the pieces makes the audience feel discomfort.

What we designed

Three pillars from the organization itself framed every idea:

Financial stabilityCommunity engagementArtistic excellence

HEIRLINE · SCAD SERV 312/321 Prototyping Experiences

Find what’s yours.

Cross-border inheritance asset discovery for the families left searching. Death is inevitable. Losing what they left you isn’t.

The system behind the screens

My roleProject lead

The brief: create a service that doesn’t exist, starting from four assigned words. I carried it to the final concept, with Renée Morales’s help and Alec Treherne in the early phase.

What I didLed the direction
  • Found the opening: a blue ocean, around €4T of unclaimed inheritance assets that no single service connects across borders.
  • Surfaced the banking stakeholder whose “convertibility” reframe unlocked the final direction.
  • Ran the memory tests, our primary validation method.
  • Made the pivot decisions that got us from a corridor to an inheritance service.

With Renée Morales and, early on, Alec Treherne · Renée also built the service blueprint, the user journey and the final prototype.

The service

“Government databases don’t talk to each other.”The villain of the story

Service blueprint

What the family sees, and what makes it possible

The line of visibility divides what the family sees from the infrastructure behind it. HEIRLINE’s value lives in the backend: invisible government APIs, partner networks and legal routing that families should never have to navigate themselves.

1SearchMulti-DB query engine and result aggregation: the databases finally talk
2Get notifiedPush notifications, then an asset report with value estimates

And then

A service
appeared.

Assets that must move between systems that don’t talk to each other. That became HEIRLINE.

The person we designed for

My father died in October. He’d lived in three countries. I didn’t even know where to start.

User interview, February 2026

Move 37 vs Move 78: we separated the AI “average” from human insight — the surprising move against the expected one — and a Google Scholar check found no published work on the mechanism.

3

Not finding is a finding

Before HEIRLINE existed, three concepts failed. Each failure told us which data we could not trust, and that narrowed the path.

Concept 1

VR chat

What we tested

We interviewed 20 people about how their 3-word answers related to each other, in a VR chat.

What didn’t make sense2–3answers before people got tired

After two or three answers people were fatigued, so the answers that followed could not be trusted.

What we learned

Too much to take in at once: cognitive overload.

Concept 2

WhatsApp prototype

What we tested

A chat-based version of the word exercise.

What didn’t make senseBiasthe format led the answers

The way we asked changed what people said. Interviews after 11 p.m. also showed a lack of seriousness.

What we learned

Interviewer bias: the format and the hour shape the data.

Concept 3

AI-written concepts

What we tested

We wrote texts from the most frequent words of the 3-word exercise, asked people to read them, and ran a memory test afterwards.

What didn’t make sense0%memory recall

Nobody remembered the concepts after the session.

What we learned

If people can’t remember it, it isn’t ready. We simplified until they could.

“The concepts selected weren’t memorable. So we simplified until they were.”Each failure narrowed the path to the service

02

The solution: three pillars

When someone dies, their assets don’t disappear. They just become invisible.

Our final deck
€4Tunclaimed inheritance assets estimated globally
2–4yrsaverage time to locate cross-border assets without help

The three pillars emerged from the data, not from our assumptions. Each one has a problem, and a part of HEIRLINE that answers it. Figures as stated in our final deck.

Behavioral1 in 3

families with cross-border inheritance never locate all assets. They don’t fail because they don’t try: no single point of access exists.

→
HEIRLINE’s answer

One search, one intake form

Type in a parent’s name once. HEIRLINE searches government databases in several countries and reports back. Stakeholders called the one-intake-form idea intuitive and necessary.

Economic40%

commission is the industry standard. Probate lawyers charge up to 40% per located asset: “a tax on grief.”

→
HEIRLINE’s answer

€180, flat

A flat subscription with full search and full claim support, transparent and built on trust, instead of a commission on what is found.

Structural74%

of families didn’t know a service like this could exist. The villain isn’t the lawyer: governments’ databases don’t talk to each other.

→
HEIRLINE’s answer

A connector that does the talking

HEIRLINE sits between registries and banks in different jurisdictions, with one family in the middle, and routes the search for them.

“The bank said go to the solicitor. The solicitor said go to the notary. The notary said go to the bank.” Secondary research, bereaved family forum.

1Fragmented databases

Property titles, tax records and bank accounts live in separate systems.

2No neutral orchestrator

No service connects governments, banks and legal partners for the family.

3Decision fatigue

Grieving families shouldn’t have to become experts in international probate law.

First ideaA search tool

Type in a name, get results.

  • can’t navigate jurisdiction
  • can’t submit forms across borders
  • can’t hold a grieving family’s hand
→
The realizationDesigning trust

At the worst moment of someone’s life.

Death is inevitable. The administrative chaos that follows it is not.

Expert Advisor, March 2026
03

Did it stick?

The usual wayUp to 40%commission per located asset
vs
HEIRLINE€180flat subscription

9/10

stakeholders remembered the core concept after one explanation. The test framing that made it stick: “Google for dead people’s money.”

The reframe

HEIRLINE is less about finding assets and more about designing trust at the worst moment of someone’s life.

Next time

  • Interview bereaved families earlier
  • Test the emotional arc, not only the mechanism
  • Recruit strangers to avoid friendly-user bias

A physical problem people recognize

“My dad died, stuff is scattered, I don’t know where to look.”

A clear villain

“Government databases don’t talk to each other.”

The one thing to remember

“It finds what you didn’t know existed.”

What I took from it

Insight 1Language is a design materialWe spent weeks saying “commercial corridors” before realizing nobody outside our studio used that phrase.
Insight 2Not finding is a findingThree iterations failed before HEIRLINE emerged. Every dead end was data.
Insight 3The villain makes the serviceOnce we named the structural problem, the service almost designed itself.
Insight 4Memory is the minimum viable metricIf people can’t remember what you built after one conversation, the concept isn’t ready. 9/10 retention became our north star.
Insight 5The personal layerDeath is inevitable. The administrative chaos that follows it is not. That’s what makes this solvable, and I design for the moments when systems should get out of the way and let people grieve.
Curious?

How did we get here?

From four words and no client to a service that connects systems that don’t talk. The research is behind the fold-out above.

Packed schedules get in the way of well-being.

Problem

Students struggle to balance mental, physical and spiritual health under academic pressure. They need a clear, community-based solution that fits a busy day.
